CURRENT SCRIPT, EXACT LAST VERSION PROVIDED TO USER:
SLIDES 1–6: SAROSH

Slide 1
Meet a hypothetical founder in the world after AI.
Four-point-two million raised. Twelve thousand customers. Thirty deployments a week. Zero security hires.
All vibe-coded, but everything works.

Slide 2
But working isn’t the same as being secure.
One missing permission check lets someone access another customer’s data.

Slide 3
And everything broke. Customers leave. Funding disappears. Eighteen jobs are lost. The company closes, and you owe $2.4 million.
The impact isn’t just broken software. It’s someone’s livelihood, their team, and their customers’ trust.

Slide 4
AI makes building easier, but security expertise doesn’t automatically follow.
Why not ask AI to secure it too? Because generating a fix isn’t the same as independently checking it.
Veracode’s 2025 benchmark found that 45% of AI-generated samples failed security tests.
Separately, Check Point reported weekly attack attempts increased roughly seventy percent between 2023 and 2025. That doesn’t prove AI coding caused the increase.

Slides 5–6
The problem is simple: AI lets small startup teams ship code faster than they can secure it.
Our ideal customer is a small, founder-led SaaS startup using AI without a dedicated cybersecurity team.
Our hypothesis is that code output is outpacing security coverage.
That’s our life-after-AI connection: the ability to create expanded, but protection hasn’t kept pace.

SLIDES 7–11: SRIHITH

Slides 7–8
Introducing Ari.
Ari connects code review, seven security specialists, and monitoring through shared code context.
Scout maps. Probe tests. Trace connects evidence. Diagnose identifies causes. Patch proposes repairs. Fortify recommends guardrails. Verify independently retests.
Recognized standards make findings understandable and verifiable.

Slide 9
Red investigates. Blue repairs. Verify checks independently, with repairs requiring human approval.
Code memory retains evidence for future reassessment. Our Defense Lab studies defensive recommendations through reinforcement learning in simulation, not autonomous production responses.

Slide 10
Snyk, Semgrep and GitHub already find vulnerabilities and suggest fixes.
Our proposed advantage is connecting business intent, attack investigation and independent verification for small teams.
Our tradeoffs are assessment costs and human review. Comparative performance still needs validation.

Slide 11
The core action is simple: connect a repository, review evidence, and approve a proposed repair.
Keyboard access, clear labels and reduced motion support accessibility.
Verification produces a proposed repair, independent test results and saved evidence.
The full-chain prototype currently uses scripted AI responses.

PROTOTYPE DEMO AFTER SLIDE 11: VIHAAN
[ADD TEXT HERE: Demonstrate the weakness, proposed repair, human approval and independent verification. Clearly identify live, recorded, scripted and simulated portions.]

SLIDES 12–16: SAI

Slide 12
[ADD VERIFIED VC FEEDBACK HERE. Otherwise omit this portion.]
Jordan, CTO of Harborseed Studio, reported that after reviewing and applying Ari’s suggested fix, the injection attack stopped working while existing search tests passed.
He valued a reproducible example, not just another alert.

Slide 13: Pricing → Costs → Forecast → Funding
Our pilot plans offer seven assessments for $49.99, twenty for $129.99, and sixty for $359.99, with volume discounts.
Growth’s modeled delivery cost is approximately $81, leaving a 38% contribution margin before shared expenses.
Starting with five unpaid pilots, we model forty-two new paid accounts monthly. This planning target divides ChartMogul’s median two-year milestone to one thousand B2B subscribers by twenty-four; it is not an observed monthly average.
Under that scenario, monthly cash coverage occurs in month two, and earlier losses recover in month three.
Our six founders initially fund the $500 monthly shared-tool budget, take no salaries and reinvest surplus. Founder pay, acquisition spending and extra usage are excluded.

Slide 14
Using Census software-publisher counts and Growth pricing, our broad opportunity is approximately $20.7 million annually, with a $6.6 million starting segment.
One hundred to two hundred customers would represent roughly $156,000 to $312,000 in annual recurring revenue. These are proxies and targets, not traction.

Slide 15
Our initial outreach target is one hundred companies, thirty conversations, ten design partners, five pilots and three total paying customers.
We’ll measure findings, repair acceptance, costs and time saved before expanding. This recruitment goal is separate from our expanded growth scenario.

Slide 16
Month one: validate live-provider assessments with five pilots.
Months two and three: test a hosted beta and paid conversion.
Months four to six: expand to multiple repositories after measuring trust and costs.
Our existing team and capped compute support these stages. Findings reliability, conversion and permissions are key risks. Enterprise follows proven controls and support capacity.

SLIDES 17–18: SAROSH

Slide 17
Our team combines Georgia House business-growth research, MIT agentic research, Georgia Tech reinforcement learning and industrial engineering, Apex146 data science, and 3Lines venture-capital experience.

Slide 18
AI gave a founder the power to build.
One weakness put everything at risk.
Seven specialists investigate and repair.
Red attacks. Blue defends.
Founder-focused pricing supports adoption.
Proof guides our path to scale.
From the first line of code to the next release. One connected defense.
That’s Ari.
